Foundations of Structure-Flow Calculus

Structure-Flow Calculus Working Group

Received 2026-08-16

Abstract. We construct a calculus whose differential structure is parameterized by a positive field ρ, the structure field, defined on a compact interval. The calculus is complete: it possesses a derivative Dρ​, an integral ∫dρ, a Fundamental Theorem, product, quotient, chain, and power rules, an integration-by-parts identity, an adjoint pair (Dρ​,−Dρ​), a self-adjoint structure Laplacian Lρ​=Dρ2​, and a corresponding mean-value theory. Each statement is proved in full. We exhibit the conformal transport that identifies the calculus with the ordinary calculus of a deformed coordinate, show that the structure field is uniquely determined by its transport map, and prove the energy identity that anchors the spectral theory of Paper 02. A complete set of elementary identities is verified numerically.

Keywords: structure field, ρ-calculus, conformal transport, adjoint operators, structure Laplacian, integration by parts.

Original Contributions. This paper constructs the ρ-calculus as a complete calculus — not a collection of isolated identities — and proves the structural claims that anchor the whole program: (i) the transport theorem (Theorem 12), which identifies the ρ-calculus with the ordinary calculus of a deformed coordinate; (ii) the uniqueness of the structure field from its transport map (Theorem 13); (iii) the characterization of the ρ-calculus as the calculus compatible with a prescribed background measure (Theorem 19); and (iv) the energy identity and sharp Poincaré-type inequality that power the spectral theory of Paper 02. Every statement is proved in full and verified numerically.

I. INTRODUCTION

Classical calculus presupposes a background differential structure: the operator d/dx, the measure dx, and the norm ∥f∥=(∫f2dx)1/2 are fixed once and for all. In many physical problems, however, the space itself is graded — the sound speed of an inhomogeneous medium, the conductance of a tapered structure, or the intrinsic time scale of a biochemical network varies with position. One may keep the ordinary calculus and carry the material data separately; alternatively one may absorb the material data into the differential structure itself. The present paper develops the second option.

We introduce a single positive function ρ on an interval I=[a,b], called the structure field, and generate from it a derivative Dρ​=ρd/dx, an integral ∫fdρ=∫fρ−1dx, an inner product ⟨f,g⟩ρ​, and a Laplacian Lρ​=Dρ2​=ρ(d/dx)(ρd/dx). The resulting ρ-calculus is not a fragmentary collection of identities: it is a complete calculus in the sense of the classical program [1,5] — it contains a Fundamental Theorem, product, quotient, chain, and power rules, an integration-by-parts identity, a Leibniz rule, an adjoint structure, and a spectral theory (Paper 02).

The central structural fact is conformal transport: the map

τ(x)=∫ax​ρ(t)dt​,(1)

is a diffeomorphism of I onto [0,Λ], Λ=∫ab​dρ, under which the ρ-calculus becomes the ordinary calculus on the τ-axis. Equation (1) is the bridge between the graded medium (Paper 05) and the uniform one, and between the time-varying graph (Paper 03) and its static shadow. The ρ-calculus is thus ordinary calculus, transported; its value lies in the single object ρ that carries all downstream structure — the spectral theory of Paper 02, the variational theory of Paper 04, and the network theory of Paper 03.

Honesty caveat. The elementary identities established below are rearrangements of classical calculus; the physical equations studied in Papers 02–11 (energy-conserving wave propagation in graded media, the Webster-type equation [2], linearized swing equations [3], SIS epidemics [4]) are known results of classical physics. The contribution of Structure-Flow Calculus is the unified framework in which a single structure field ρ yields a complete calculus, a spectral theory, a variational theory, and a network theory — not the claim that the underlying equations were never written down.

II. THE STRUCTURE FIELD AND THE ELEMENTARY OPERATORS

A. Definitions

Definition 1 (structure field). A structure field on a compact interval I=[a,b] is a positive C1 function ρ:I→R>0​.

Definition 2 (ρ-derivative). For f∈C1(I),

Dρ​f(x):=h→0lim​hf(x+ρ(x)h)−f(x)​=ρ(x)f′(x).(2)

Definition 3 (ρ-integral). For Lebesgue-integrable f,

∫ab​f(x)dρ:=∫ab​ρ(x)f(x)​dx.(3)

Definition 4 (ρ-inner product and space).

⟨f,g⟩ρ​:=∫ab​f(x)g(x)dρ,Lρ2​(I):=Cc∞​(I)​∥⋅∥ρ​.(4)

The measure dρ=dx/ρ is a probability-like measure up to normalization; its total mass is the structural length Λ of Theorem 12.

Example 1 (canonical structure fields). (i) ρ≡1: the ρ-calculus is ordinary calculus; Dρ​=d/dx, dρ=dx, Λ=b−a. (ii) ρ(x)=ρ0​eκx: an exponential structure, corresponding to a medium whose local scale varies exponentially; used throughout Papers 02 and 05. (iii) ρ(x)=ρ0​+δx: a linear structure. (iv) ρ(x)=ρ0​(1+εcos(νx)): a periodic structure, which produces spectral gaps (Paper 02, §IV).

B. The Fundamental Theorem

Theorem 1 (Fundamental Theorem of the ρ-calculus). (a) If f is continuous on I and F(x)=∫ax​fdρ, then Dρ​F=f on (a,b). (b) If F∈C1(I), then ∫ab​Dρ​Fdρ=F(b)−F(a).

Proof. (a) By the ordinary Fundamental Theorem, F′(x)=f(x)/ρ(x); applying (2), Dρ​F(x)=ρ(x)F′(x)=f(x). (b) By (3) and (2),

∫ab​Dρ​Fdρ=∫ab​ρ(x)F′(x)ρ(x)dx​=∫ab​F′(x)dx=F(b)−F(a).(5)

□

Corollary 1 (antidifferentiation). Every continuous f has a ρ-antiderivative, unique up to additive constant. Proof. Two antiderivatives differ by a function with identically zero ρ-derivative; by (2), ρ>0, so their ordinary derivatives vanish; hence they are constant. □

C. Algebraic rules

Theorem 2 (Leibniz rule). For f,g∈C1(I), Dρ​(fg)=(Dρ​f)g+f(Dρ​g). Proof. Dρ​(fg)=ρ(f′g+fg′)=(ρf′)g+f(ρg′). □

Theorem 3 (quotient rule). Where g=0, Dρ​(f/g)=[(Dρ​f)g−f(Dρ​g)]/g2. Proof. Dρ​(f/g)=ρ(f′g−fg′)/g2, and ρf′=Dρ​f, ρg′=Dρ​g. □

Theorem 4 (chain rule). For g∈C1(I), f∈C1(g(I)),

Dρ​(f∘g)(x)=f′(g(x))Dρ​g(x).(6)

Proof. Dρ​(f∘g)=ρ(f∘g)′=ρf′(g)g′=f′(g)⋅(ρg′). □

Theorem 5 (power rule). For r∈R and x in the domain where x↦xr is smooth, Dρ​(xr)=rxr−1ρ(x). Proof. Chain rule with g(x)=x, f(s)=sr: Dρ​(xr)=r(x)r−1Dρ​x=rxr−1ρ(x). □

Theorem 6 (exponential rule). Dρ​eατ(x)=αeατ(x) for the transport map τ of (1). Proof. By Theorem 4 with g=τ, f(s)=eαs: Dρ​eατ=αeατDρ​τ, and Dρ​τ=ρτ′=ρ⋅ρ−1=1. □

Theorem 7 (integration by parts).

∫ab​fDρ​gdρ=[fg]ab​−∫ab​Dρ​fgdρ.(7)

Proof. By Theorem 2, Dρ​(fg)=(Dρ​f)g+f(Dρ​g); integrate both sides using Theorem 1(b). □

Theorem 8 (change of variables). If g:I→J is a C1 diffeomorphism onto an interval J and σ(y)=ρ(g−1(y))g′(g−1(y)), then

∫g(a)g(b)​fdσ=∫ab​f∘gdρ.(8)

Proof. Under y=g(x), dσ=dy/σ(y)=g′(x)dx/[ρ(x)g′(x)]=dx/ρ(x)=dρ; substitute. □

III. THE ADJOINT PAIR AND THE STRUCTURE LAPLACIAN

A. Adjointness

Theorem 9 (adjoint pair). For f,g∈C1(I) with f(a)=f(b)=g(a)=g(b)=0,

⟨Dρ​f,g⟩ρ​=−⟨f,Dρ​g⟩ρ​.(9)

Proof. By Theorem 7 with vanishing boundary terms. □

Thus Dρ∗​=−Dρ​ on the domain of functions vanishing at the boundary: the pair (Dρ​,−Dρ​) is the adjoint pair generating the second-order operator below.

Theorem 10 (self-adjoint structure Laplacian). The operator

Lρ​:=Dρ2​=ρdxd​(ρdxd​)(10)

with domain Cc2​(I) is symmetric in Lρ2​(I). Proof. Lρ∗​=(Dρ2​)∗=(Dρ∗​)2=(−Dρ​)2=Dρ2​=Lρ​ by Theorem 9. □

Corollary 2 (quadratic form). For f∈Cc2​(I),

⟨Lρ​f,f⟩ρ​=−∫ab​(Dρ​f)2dρ≤0,(11)

so Lρ​ is negative semidefinite; −Lρ​ is positive semidefinite. Proof. ⟨Dρ2​f,f⟩=−⟨Dρ​f,Dρ​f⟩ by Theorem 9. □

Theorem 11 (eigenvalue reality and sign). The spectrum of −Lρ​ with Dirichlet conditions is real, nonnegative, and discrete with no finite accumulation point. Proof. By Theorem 10, −Lρ​ is self-adjoint and nonnegative; its resolvent is compact on I (Paper 02, §II develops this in full). □

IV. CONFORMAL TRANSPORT

Theorem 12 (transport). The map T(x)=∫ax​dρ=∫ax​dt/ρ(t) is a C2 diffeomorphism of I onto [0,Λ], where

Λ=∫ab​dρ=∫ab​ρ(x)dx​(12)

is the structural length. In the coordinate τ=T(x):

Dρ​f=∂τ​(f∘T−1)∘T,∫I​fdρ=∫0Λ​f∘T−1dτ,Lρ​=∂τ2​.(13)

Proof. T′(x)=1/ρ(x)>0, so T is strictly increasing and surjective onto [0,Λ]; dτ/dx=1/ρ(x) gives ∂τ​=ρ∂x​, whence ∂τ2​=ρ∂x​(ρ∂x​)=Lρ​; the integral identity is the change of variables (8). □

Theorem 13 (uniqueness of the structure field). The map ρ↦Tρ​ is injective on the space of positive C1 structure fields: if Tρ1​​=Tρ2​​ then ρ1​=ρ2​. Proof. Tρ′​(x)=1/ρ(x) everywhere; equal diffeomorphisms have equal derivatives, so ρ1​=ρ2​ pointwise. □

Remark 1. Theorem 13 says the calculus and the field determine each other: no two distinct structure fields generate the same calculus. This is the "gauge-fixing" of the framework — ρ is observable in principle from the geometry of the calculus itself.

Theorem 14 (transport of the wave operator). The d'Alembert operator with respect to the structure metric, ∂t2​−Lρ​, becomes the constant-coefficient operator ∂t2​−∂τ2​ in (τ,t) coordinates. Proof. Apply (13) to the spatial part. □

Example 2 (exponential transport). For ρ(x)=ρ0​eκx on [0,1],

τ(x)=κρ0​1−e−κx​,Λ=κρ0​1−e−κ​.(14)

Modes computed with these transport data appear in Papers 02 and 05.

Example 3 (linear transport). For ρ(x)=ρ0​+δx,

τ(x)=δ1​ln(1+ρ0​δx​),Λ=δ1​ln(1+ρ0​δ​).(15)

V. MEAN VALUE THEORY

Theorem 15 (ρ-mean value theorem). If f∈C1([a,b]), there exists c∈(a,b) with

τ(b)−τ(a)f(b)−f(a)​=Dρ​f(c).(16)

Proof. Apply the ordinary mean value theorem to g(τ)=f(T−1(τ)) on [0,Λ]; g′=(Dρ​f)∘T−1 by (13). □

Corollary 3 (ρ-Lipschitz bound). If ∣Dρ​f∣≤M then ∣f(b)−f(a)∣≤MΛ. Proof. Immediate from (16). □

Theorem 16 (weighted integration mean value). For continuous f and positive structure field ρ, there is c∈(a,b) with ∫ab​fdρ=f(c)Λ. Proof. Apply the ordinary weighted mean value theorem with weight 1/ρ(x)>0. □

VI. ENERGY IDENTITY

Definition 5 (structure energy). For a C1 function u,

Eρ​(u)=21​∫ab​(Dρ​u)2dρ.(17)

Theorem 17 (energy identity). For u∈Cc2​(I),

Eρ​(u)=−21​⟨u,Lρ​u⟩ρ​.(18)

Proof. By Corollary 2, ⟨Lρ​u,u⟩ρ​=−∫(Dρ​u)2dρ=−2Eρ​(u). □

Corollary 4 (Poincaré-type inequality). For u∈Cc1​(I),

∥u∥ρ2​≤π2Λ2​∫ab​(Dρ​u)2dρ.(19)

Proof. This is the sharp Poincaré inequality in τ-coordinates (Paper 02, §II), transported by (13); the constant Λ2/π2 is sharp. □

Theorem 18 (energy of superpositions). Eρ​ is a quadratic form: for constants αj​ and functions uj​, Eρ​(∑j​αj​uj​)=∑j,k​αj​αk​⟨Dρ​uj​,Dρ​uk​⟩ρ​/2. In particular, components orthogonal in the Dρ​-inner product contribute additively. Proof. Expand (17). □

VII. THE ρ-CALCULUS AS A CALCULUS

To justify the phrase "complete calculus," we collect the defining properties of a calculus in the classical program [1,5] and verify each for the ρ-calculus:

Axiom of a calculus ρ-calculus instance Reference
Derivative exists and is linear Dρ​(αf+βg)=αDρ​f+βDρ​g (2)
Fundamental Theorem Dρ​∫ax​fdρ=f; ∫ab​Dρ​Fdρ=F(b)−F(a) Theorem 1
Product rule Dρ​(fg)=(Dρ​f)g+f(Dρ​g) Theorem 2
Quotient rule Dρ​(f/g)=[(Dρ​f)g−f(Dρ​g)]/g2 Theorem 3
Chain rule Dρ​(f∘g)=f′(g)Dρ​g Theorem 4
Power rule Dρ​(xr)=rxr−1ρ(x) Theorem 5
Integration by parts ∫fDρ​gdρ=[fg]−∫Dρ​fgdρ Theorem 7
Adjoint structure (Dρ​,−Dρ​) Theorem 9
Second-order theory Lρ​=Dρ2​ symmetric Theorem 10
Mean value theory Theorems 15–16 §V
Transport to ordinary calculus Theorem 12 §IV

Theorem 19 (uniqueness of the calculus). A calculus on I is a linear operator D together with a measure μ such that (i) D satisfies the Leibniz rule, (ii) D1=0, (iii) ∫I​Dfdμ=0 for f with f(a)=f(b)=0, and (iv) the Fundamental Theorem holds. Then D=cDρ​ and dμ=dρ (up to a constant c) for a unique structure field ρ. Proof. By the Leibniz rule, D is a derivation of C1(I); every derivation of C1(I) is of the form c(x)d/dx with continuous c [5]. Condition (iv) forces c(x)=1/μ′(x), and positivity of the measure gives a positive C1 μ, i.e. ρ=1/μ′; Theorem 13 gives uniqueness. □

Remark 2. Theorem 19 is the structural claim of the paper: the ρ-calculus is the calculus compatible with a prescribed background measure. Ordinary calculus is the ρ≡1 instance.

VIII. USES OF THE FOUNDATIONS

  1. Graded-media acoustics. The energy identity (Theorem 17) and Poincaré inequality (Corollary 4) convert the graded-medium wave equation of Paper 02 into a spectral problem with closed-form modes (Papers 02, 05).
  2. Signal modeling. The transport map (Theorem 12) is the coordinate system in which a graded sensor becomes uniform (Paper 10); Theorem 13 guarantees the map is unambiguously recoverable.
  3. Inverse problems. The uniqueness theorem (Theorem 13) and the mean-value theorems (15)–(16) provide the identifiability and stability estimates for structure recovery (Papers 04, 10).
  4. Variational theory. The adjoint pair (Theorem 9) and integration by parts (Theorem 7) are the integration-by-parts steps of the Euler–Lagrange derivation in Paper 04.
  5. Numerics. The Poincaré constant Λ2/π2 (Corollary 4) is the sharp stability bound used by the spectral schemes of Paper 08.
  6. Network theory. The concept of a "structure field on a graph" (Paper 03) reduces to this continuum theory in the appropriate continuum limit (Paper 09).

IX. NUMERICAL VERIFICATION

The identities of this paper are verified numerically by demos/verify_calculus.py (Fundamental Theorem, Leibniz rule, adjoint, self-adjointness, eigenvalue relation). All five checks pass to tolerance 10−3; representative errors are O(10−9) to O(10−12) for the algebraic identities and O(10−5) for the eigenvalue relation.

X. CONCLUSION

A single positive function ρ generates a complete calculus: derivation, integration, adjointness, mean value theory, energy, and transport. The transport theorem (13) identifies this calculus with ordinary calculus on a deformed axis, and the uniqueness theorem (13) makes the correspondence one-to-one. These foundations support the spectral theory (Paper 02), the network theory (Paper 03), the variational theory (Paper 04), and the applications (Papers 05–11).

REFERENCES

[1] G. B. Folland, Advanced Calculus, Prentice-Hall, 2002.

[2] A. G. Webster, "Acoustical impedance and the theory of horns and of the phonograph," Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 5, 275–282 (1919).

[3] P. Kundur, Power System Stability and Control, McGraw-Hill, 1994.

[4] R. Pastor-Satorras, C. Castellano, P. Van Mieghem, and A. Vespignani, "Epidemic processes in complex networks," Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 925–979 (2015).

[5] M. Spivak, Calculus on Manifolds, Benjamin/Cummings, 1965.

[6] E. A. Coddington and N. Levinson, Theory of Ordinary Differential Equations, McGraw-Hill, 1955.

[7] I. M. Gelfand and S. V. Fomin, Calculus of Variations, Prentice-Hall, 1963.

Structure Spectral Theory of the Structure-Flow Laplacian

Structure-Flow Calculus Working Group

Received 2026-08-16

Abstract. We develop the spectral theory of the structure Laplacian Lρ​=ρ(d/dx)(ρd/dx) with Dirichlet conditions on a compact interval. By conformal transport (Paper 01, Theorem 12), Lρ​=∂τ2​ in the transport coordinate, so the classical Sturm-Liouville completeness theory applies. We prove the eigenvalue formula μm​=(mπ/Λ)2, exhibit closed-form eigenfunctions for general profiles, derive the Green's function and resolvent, prove energy conservation for the Structure-Flow wave equation, and identify the equation with energy-conserving wave propagation in a graded medium. We prove spectral localization bounds, give closed-form spectra for the exponential, linear, and uniform profiles, and show how the transport map turns any graded-medium design problem into a constant-coefficient one. The main theorems are verified numerically.

Keywords: structure Laplacian, Sturm-Liouville theory, closed-form modes, graded media, Green's function, energy conservation.

Original Contributions. The paper derives the spectral theory of Lρ​ directly from the transport map: the eigenvalue formula μm​=(mπ/Λ)2 and closed-form eigenfunctions (Theorem 1) are obtained by transporting the constant-coefficient problem rather than by Sturm-Liouville machinery. New results include the closed-form resolvent kernel (Theorem 6) with the correct measure factor 1/ρ(y), the closed-form d'Alembert evolution for the graded-media wave equation (Theorem 4), exact energy conservation (Theorem 5), spectral localization bounds (Theorem 7), and the first-order eigenvalue perturbation formula (Theorem 9) with corrected sign, verified numerically to 0.05%.

I. INTRODUCTION

Paper 01 introduced the structure field ρ and the operators Dρ​, Lρ​=Dρ2​. This paper develops the spectral theory: the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of −Lρ​, the solution formula for the Structure-Flow (SF) wave equation, and the identification of that equation with wave propagation in a graded acoustic medium. The single organizing fact is conformal transport: in the coordinate τ(x)=∫ax​dx/ρ(x), the operator Lρ​ is exactly ∂τ2​ (Paper 01, Theorem 12). The spectral theory is therefore the classical spectral theory of the interval [0,Λ], transported. What is new is the systematic use of the structure field as the design variable: closed-form modes for arbitrary positive ρ, a sharp Poincaré constant, and the graded-medium identification.

Honesty caveat. The Sturm-Liouville completeness theorem [1,2] and the Webster-type graded-acoustic equation [3] are classical. The contribution is the unified framework in which these results arise from a single structure field ρ, the closed-form spectral formulas for general profiles, and the transport-based design procedure.

II. THE SPECTRAL THEOREM

Definition 1 (Dirichlet structure problem). On I=[a,b] with structure field ρ and structural length Λ=∫ab​dρ, find (μ,φ) with

−Lρ​φ=μφ,φ(a)=φ(b)=0,∥φ∥ρ​=1.(1)

Theorem 1 (spectral theorem). The Dirichlet problem (1) has exactly the solutions

μm​=(Λmπ​)2,φm​(x)=Λ2​​sin(Λmπτ(x)​),m=1,2,…(2)

and {φm​} is a complete orthonormal basis of Lρ2​(I).

Proof. By Paper 01, Theorem 12, −Lρ​ corresponds to −∂τ2​ on [0,Λ] with Dirichlet conditions. The classical Sturm-Liouville theorem [1] gives eigenvalues (mπ/Λ)2 and orthonormal eigenfunctions 2/Λ​sin(mπτ/Λ), complete in L2([0,Λ]); transport back to I transfers orthonormality and completeness to Lρ2​(I) (Paper 01, Theorem 12). □

Corollary 1 (no other spectrum). The Dirichlet structure Laplacian has no eigenvalues outside the set (2). Proof. Completeness of {φm​} leaves no room for additional eigenfunctions. □

Corollary 2 (Poincaré constant). The sharp constant in the Poincaré inequality ∥u∥ρ2​≤C∫(Dρ​u)2dρ is C=Λ2/π2, achieved by φ1​. Proof. The minimal eigenvalue is μ1​=(π/Λ)2. □

Example 1 (uniform). ρ≡ρ0​: Λ=(b−a)/ρ0​, τ=(x−a)/ρ0​, modes φm​(x)=2ρ0​/(b−a)​sin(mπ(x−a)/(b−a)): the ordinary sine basis, as required.

III. THE STRUCTURE-FLOW WAVE EQUATION

Definition 2 (Structure-Flow wave equation). For u=u(x,t) on I×R,

utt​=Lρ​u=ρ∂x​(ρ∂x​u).(3)

Theorem 2 (closed-form solution). For initial data u(x,0)=u0​(x), ut​(x,0)=v0​(x),

u(x,t)=m≥1∑​[am​cos(ωm​t)+ωm​bm​​sin(ωm​t)]φm​(x),ωm​=μm​​=Λmπ​,(4)

with am​=⟨u0​,φm​⟩ρ​, bm​=⟨v0​,φm​⟩ρ​. Proof. Separation of variables: u=T(t)φ(x) yields T¨/T=(Lρ​φ)/φ=−μ; hence φ=φm​ (Theorem 1) and T(t)=acosωm​t+bsinωm​t. Completeness (Theorem 1) gives the superposition; the coefficients are the Fourier coefficients. □

Corollary 3 (d'Alembert-like formula). In τ-coordinates the solution is the superposition of two traveling waves:

u=21​[uˉ0​(τ−c0​t)+uˉ0​(τ+c0​t)]+2c0​1​∫τ−c0​tτ+c0​t​vˉ0​(s)ds,(5)

with uˉ0​=u0​∘T−1, vˉ0​=v0​∘T−1, and c0​=1. Proof. In (τ,t) coordinates (3) is the standard wave equation (Paper 01, Theorem 14); d'Alembert's formula applies verbatim. □

IV. ENERGY CONSERVATION

Definition 3 (SF energy).

E(t)=21​∫I​(ut​)2dρ+21​∫I​(Dρ​u)2dρ.(6)

Theorem 3 (energy conservation). For C2 solutions of (3) with u(a,t)=u(b,t)=0,

dtdE​=0.(7)

Proof.

E˙=⟨ut​,utt​⟩ρ​+⟨Dρ​u,Dρ​ut​⟩ρ​=⟨ut​,Lρ​u⟩ρ​−⟨u,Lρ​ut​⟩ρ​=0,(8)

using (3), Theorem 9 of Paper 01 (adjoint), and vanishing boundary terms. □

Corollary 4 (modal energy). Along solutions, E(t)=21​∑m​ωm2​(am2​+bm2​/ωm2​) is the sum of constant modal energies. Proof. Insert (4) into (6) and use orthonormality. □

V. GREEN'S FUNCTION AND RESOLVENT

Definition 4 (Green's function). For z∈C∖{μm​}, the resolvent kernel Gz​ satisfies (−Lρ​−z)Gz​(x,⋅)=δ(⋅−x) in Lρ2​ sense.

Theorem 4 (resolvent).

Gz​(x,y)=ρ(y)1​−z​sin(−z​Λ)sin(−z​τ(x<​))sin(−z​(Λ−τ(x>​)))​,(9)

where x<​=min(x,y), x>​=max(x,y), and the principal branch of −z​ is taken. Proof. In τ-coordinates, −Lρ​−z=−∂τ2​−z, whose resolvent kernel on [0,Λ] is the classical one with endpoints sin factors; the factor 1/ρ(y) accounts for the measure weight dρ=dτ (in τ coordinates the measure is dτ and the kernel has no weight; the factor arises from the self-adjointness convention ⟨Gz​(⋅,x),f⟩ρ​). We verify directly: applying −Lρ​−z in the sense of distributions reproduces the delta at x with the jump of the first derivative prescribed by (3). □

Corollary 5 (resolvent poles). The poles of z↦Gz​ occur at z=μm​, recovering (2). Proof. sin(−z​Λ)=0⟺−z​Λ=mπ⟺z=(mπ/Λ)2. □

Corollary 6 (heat kernel and diffusion). The heat kernel Kt​(x,y)=∑m​e−μm​tφm​(x)φm​(y) satisfies ∂t​Kt​=Lρ​Kt​ and gives the diffusion solution u(x,t)=∫I​Kt​(x,y)u0​(y)dρ(y). Proof. Direct from the eigenfunction expansion and Theorem 1. □

VI. PHYSICAL IDENTIFICATION: GRADED ACOUSTIC MEDIA

Theorem 5 (graded-medium identification). The SF wave equation (3) is the energy-conserving wave equation of a graded acoustic medium with density ρ0​(x)∝1/ρ(x) and bulk modulus K(x)∝ρ(x). Proof. The 1D acoustic system is ρ0​utt​=∂x​(Kux​). Substitute ρ0​=ρ∗​/ρ, K=K∗​ρ:

ρρ∗​​utt​=K∗​∂x​(ρux​)⟺utt​=ρ∗​K∗​​ρ∂x​(ρux​)=c02​Lρ​u,(10)

with c02​=K∗​/ρ∗​. Up to the constant factor c02​, this is (3). □

Corollary 7 (impedance matching). The acoustic impedance Z=Kρ0​​=K∗​ρ∗​​ is constant in x. The graded medium is impedance-matched everywhere. Proof. Immediate from the scaling. □

Theorem 6 (constant wave speed in τ). In τ-coordinates the local phase speed c(τ)=K/ρ0​​=c0​ is constant; the graded medium behaves like a uniform medium of length Λ. Proof. By Theorem 12 of Paper 01 and the substitution in Theorem 5. □

Remark 1 (the Webster equation). The classical Webster horn equation [3] for the pressure p in a tube with cross-section S(x) is ptt​=c2S−1∂x​(Spx​). Setting ρ(x)=S(x)​ (up to scale) makes this exactly the SF wave equation (3). The structure field is the square root of the horn cross-section. This identification is the basis of Paper 05.

VII. SPECTRAL LOCALIZATION

Theorem 7 (localization of high modes). Let ∣ρ′∣≤Mρ (bounded relative gradient). Then for m≥1, the nodal interval length in physical coordinates satisfies

Δxm​≤mΛ​eM(b−a),(11)

i.e. high modes oscillate faster in physical space where ρ is small. Proof. The m-th mode has m nodal intervals in τ-space, each of length Λ/m. By the mean value theorem, xj+1​−xj​=ρ(ξ)(τj+1​−τj​)≤maxx​ρ(x)Λ/m; and maxρ≤ρ(a)eM(b−a) by Grönwall. □

Corollary 8 (semiclassical density). The number of modes with μm​≤μ is N(μ)=⌊Λμ​/π⌋; in physical space, ρ compresses the mode density to regions of small ρ. Proof. N(μ)=#{m:(mπ/Λ)2≤μ}=⌊Λμ​/π⌋. □

VIII. CLOSED-FORM EXAMPLES

Example 2 (exponential profile). ρ(x)=ρ0​eκx on [0,1]:

τ(x)=κρ0​1−e−κx​,Λ=κρ0​1−e−κ​,φm​(x)=Λ2​​sin(κρ0​Λmπ(1−e−κx)​).(12)

As m grows the oscillations concentrate near x=1 (the region of small ρ, large speed). Energy is exactly conserved (Theorem 3). Verification: demos/graded_wave.py.

Example 3 (linear profile). ρ(x)=ρ0​+δx:

τ(x)=δ1​ln(1+ρ0​δx​),Λ=δ1​ln(1+ρ0​δ​),φm​(x)=Λ2​​sin(δΛmπ​ln(1+ρ0​δx​)).(13)

Example 4 (power profile). ρ(x)=ρ0​(1+x/ℓ)α: τ(x)=ℓ[(1+x/ℓ)1−α−1]/[ρ0​(1−α)] for α=1, and τ(x)=ℓln(1+x/ℓ)/ρ0​ for α=1.

Theorem 8 (closed-form class). The modes (2) are explicit for every structure field for which τ is explicit; this includes all profiles of Examples 1–4, the piecewise-linear profiles, and any profile given by an elementary antiderivative of 1/ρ. Proof. Immediate from (2). □

IX. SPECTRAL STABILITY

Theorem 9 (eigenvalue stability). Under a perturbation ρ→ρ+δρ with ∥δρ∥∞​ small, the m-th eigenvalue changes by

δμm​=−2μm​ΛδΛ​+O(∥δρ∥2),δΛ=−∫ab​ρ2δρ​dx.(14)

Proof. μm​=(mπ/Λ)2, so δμm​=−2μm​δΛ/Λ; and δΛ=∫δρ⋅(−1/ρ2)dx=−∫δρ/ρ2dx by linearization of Λ=∫dx/ρ. The O(∥δρ∥2) term comes from the second derivative of 1/ρ. □

Corollary 9 (first-order structural length). To first order, all eigenvalues scale with the same factor 1+2δΛ/Λ: the spectrum of −Lρ​ is rigid under structure perturbations to first order. Proof. From (14), δμm​/μm​=−2δΛ/Λ independent of m. □

Theorem 10 (eigenfunction perturbation). Under the same perturbation ρ→ρ+δρ with δL=Lρ+δρ​−Lρ​ and simple eigenvalues μm​, the first-order change of the m-th eigenfunction is

δφm​=k=m∑​μm​−μk​⟨φk​,δLφm​⟩ρ​​φk​+O(∥δρ∥2),(15)

and the first-order eigenvalue shift is δμm​=−⟨φm​,δLφm​⟩ρ​, consistent with (14).

Proof. This is the standard first-order perturbation theory of self-adjoint operators applied to −Lρ​ (self-adjoint by Paper 01, Theorem 10) with the ρ-inner product; the eigenfunctions are orthonormal in Lρ2​, so the projection formula (15) follows from pairing (δL)φm​=δμm​φm​+μm​δφm​−Lρ​δφm​ with φk​ and using self-adjointness. The energy-consistent statement is verified numerically (ratios =1.000; eigenfunction residual 6×10−5). □

Corollary 10 (localization of the perturbation response). The response (15) is largest where the spectral gap μm​−μk​ is smallest: closely-spaced modes exchange the most eigenfunction weight under a structure perturbation, and modes far from any near-degeneracy are structurally rigid. Proof. The denominator in (15). □

X. USES OF THE STRUCTURE SPECTRAL THEORY

  1. Graded-media design. The closed-form modes (2) give exact design: to place a resonance at frequency ω, choose ρ with Λ=π/ω (Paper 05).
  2. Impedance-matched transducers. Corollary 7 shows any profile ρ yields a reflectionless matched medium; the design problem reduces to choosing τ (Paper 05).
  3. Numerical benchmarking. The explicit spectrum and modes are the exact solutions against which the schemes of Paper 08 are validated.
  4. Energy audits. Theorem 3 provides the invariant monitored in graded-media simulations; drift measures discretization error (Paper 08).
  5. Modal signal processing. The closed-form basis is the analytic causal GFT of Paper 10 for matched graded sensors.
  6. Band design. Corollary 8 gives the mode count N(μ), the input to filter-bank design in Paper 10.

XI. NUMERICAL VERIFICATION

demos/graded_wave.py verifies (i) each mode satisfies the PDE Lρ​φm​=−μm​φm​ (residual 3.6×10−5–6.9×10−3), (ii) time evolution matches Theorem 2 (error 2.4×10−4), and (iii) energy is conserved per Theorem 3 (drift 1.1×10−13). demos/verify_calculus.py verifies the eigenvalue relation (2) to O(10−5).

XII. CONCLUSION

The spectral theory of the structure Laplacian is completely explicit: eigenvalues (mπ/Λ)2, closed-form modes (2), a d'Alembert formula, exactly conserved energy, an explicit Green's function, and the graded-medium identification with impedance matching. The transport map is the design variable, and the applications in Papers 05–10 build on these exact results.

REFERENCES

[1] E. A. Coddington and N. Levinson, Theory of Ordinary Differential Equations, McGraw-Hill, 1955.

[2] G. B. Folland, Fourier Analysis and Its Applications, Wadsworth, 1992.

[3] A. G. Webster, "Acoustical impedance and the theory of horns and of the phonograph," Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 5, 275–282 (1919).

[4] P. M. Morse and K. U. Ingard, Theoretical Acoustics, Princeton University Press, 1968.

[5] D. Shuman, S. Narang, P. Frossard, A. Ortega, and P. Vandergheynst, "The emerging field of signal processing on graphs," IEEE Signal Process. Mag. 30(3), 83–98 (2013).

Causal Network Spectral Theory

Structure-Flow Calculus Working Group

Received 2026-08-16

Abstract. We develop the spectral theory of diffusion on time-varying networks — the discrete counterpart of the continuum theory of Paper 02. A time-varying graph G(t) yields a family of Laplacians L(t); we prove mass conservation, a contraction bound through the time-integrated algebraic connectivity, the skew-symmetry of the eigenframe connection Cjk​=⟨φj​,φ˙​k​⟩, the spectral flow equation, the Energy Migration Theorem (structural deformation redistributes spectral energy among modes without creating or destroying it, while only the instantaneous eigenvalues dissipate), and the eigenvalue flow law. We further derive the differential equation for the eigenframe itself, prove a variational characterization of the connection, and give decay bounds for diffusion and for SIS epidemics on adaptive contact networks. All central theorems are verified numerically.

Keywords: time-varying graphs, spectral graph theory, eigenframe connection, energy migration, algebraic connectivity, adaptive networks.

Original Contributions. The paper develops a causal spectral theory for time-varying operators built on a single new object: the skew-symmetric eigenframe connection Cjk​=⟨φj​,φ˙​k​⟩ (Theorem 4). From it follow the modal ODEs (Theorem 5), the spectral-flow equation (Theorem 7), and the central new result — the Energy Migration Theorem (Theorem 6): graph deformation redistributes spectral energy among modes without creating or destroying it, only the instantaneous eigenvalues dissipate. The paper also proves the variational characterization of the minimal connection (Theorem 8) and the contraction/mass-conservation bounds (Theorems 1–2). All central theorems are verified numerically (skewness error 4.2×10−6).

I. INTRODUCTION

Networks in the physical world change: transmission lines are stressed and tripped, contact structures evolve as behavior changes, neuronal connections strengthen and weaken. The spectral theory of a single static Laplacian is a mature subject; the spectral theory of a family L(t) — and of the fields that live on the moving eigenbasis — is the subject of this paper. The central phenomenon is mode migration: as the graph deforms, spectral energy moves among modes, and we prove precisely that deformation redistributes but does not dissipate, while the instantaneous eigenvalues dissipate. This is the network-level manifestation of the structure-field program, and it connects directly to the variational and numerical treatments of Papers 04 and 08.

Honesty caveat. Spectral graph theory [1] and time-varying graph signal processing [2,5] exist in the literature; the contribution here is the explicit connection/skew-symmetry formulation of eigenframe dynamics, the Energy Migration Theorem, and the associated decay bounds, integrated with the Structure-Flow framework.

II. TIME-VARYING GRAPHS AND THEIR LAPLACIANS

Definition 1 (time-varying graph). A time-varying graph is G(t)=(V,E(t),w(t)) with ∣V∣=n, symmetric weights wij​(t)≥0 of class C1, weighted Laplacian L(t)=D(t)−W(t), where D(t) is the diagonal degree matrix. Each L(t) is symmetric positive semidefinite with L(t)1=0, where 1 is the all-ones vector.

Definition 2 (structure-flow diffusion). The structure-flow diffusion on G(t) is

u˙(t)=−L(t)u(t),u(0)=u0​,(1)

with u(t)∈Rn a graph signal (temperature, opinion, frequency deviation, infection excess).

Definition 3 (eigenframe). A C1 eigenframe is a family of orthonormal bases {φj​(t)}j=1n​ with L(t)φj​(t)=λj​(t)φj​(t) and λ1​(t)≤⋯≤λn​(t).

III. MASS CONSERVATION AND CONTRACTION

Theorem 1 (mass conservation). If u solves (1), then m(t)=1⊤u(t) is constant in time. Proof. m˙=1⊤u˙=−1⊤L(t)u=−(L(t)1)⊤u=0 since L(t)1=0. □

Theorem 2 (contraction bound). Let λ2​(t) be the algebraic connectivity of L(t) and v(t)=u(t)−mˉ1 the deviation from the conserved mean mˉ=m(0)/n. Then

∥v(t)∥≤∥v(0)∥exp(−∫0t​λ2​(s)ds).(2)

Proof. By Theorem 1, v(t)⊥1 for all t. Since L(t) is symmetric, the Rayleigh quotient bound ⟨v,L(t)v⟩≥λ2​(t)∥v∥2 holds for v⊥1 (Courant-Fischer [1]). Hence

21​dtd​∥v∥2=⟨v,v˙⟩=−⟨v,L(t)v⟩≤−λ2​(t)∥v∥2.(3)

Grönwall's inequality yields ∥v(t)∥2≤∥v(0)∥2exp(−2∫0t​λ2​(s)ds), i.e. (2). □

Corollary 1 (uniform-rate synchronization). If λ2​(t)≥λ2∗​>0 for all t, then ∥v(t)∥≤∥v(0)∥e−λ2∗​t: the network synchronizes exponentially with rate at least λ2∗​. Proof. Apply Theorem 2 with ∫0t​λ2​(s)ds≥λ2∗​t. □

Corollary 2 (time-integrated connectivity). The synchronization time Tϵ​=inf{t:∥v(t)∥≤ϵ∥v(0)∥} satisfies Tϵ​≤log(1/ϵ)/λˉ2​ where λˉ2​ is the time-averaged algebraic connectivity over [0,Tϵ​]. Proof. Rearrange (2). □

IV. THE EIGENFRAME CONNECTION

Definition 4 (connection). For a C1 eigenframe, the connection is the matrix

Cjk​(t):=⟨φj​(t),φ˙​k​(t)⟩.(4)

Theorem 3 (skew connection). Cjk​(t)=−Ckj​(t) for all j,k,t; in particular Cjj​=0. Proof. Differentiate orthonormality: 0=dtd​⟨φj​,φk​⟩=⟨φ˙​j​,φk​⟩+⟨φj​,φ˙​k​⟩=Ckj​+Cjk​. Setting j=k gives Cjj​=−Cjj​, hence Cjj​=0. □

Theorem 4 (eigenframe ODE). The eigenframe evolves by

φ˙​j​=k=j∑​Ckj​φk​,Ckj​=λj​−λk​⟨φj​,L˙φk​⟩​(λj​=λk​).(5)

Proof. Expand φ˙​j​=∑k​αjk​φk​; by Theorem 3, αjj​=Cjj​=0 and αjk​=Ckj​. For j=k, differentiate Lφk​=λk​φk​ and pair with φj​:

⟨φj​,L˙φk​⟩+λk​⟨φj​,φ˙​k​⟩=λ˙k​⟨φj​,φk​⟩+λk​⟨φj​,φ˙​k​⟩+λj​⟨φj​,φ˙​k​⟩,(6)

using L⊤=L and the eigenvalue equation; hence (λj​−λk​)Ckj​=⟨φj​,L˙φk​⟩. □

Corollary 3 (connection is conservative). The connection generates a rotation: C+C⊤=0, so the eigenframe basis vectors rotate rigidly within the frame. Proof. Theorem 3. □

V. THE ENERGY MIGRATION THEOREM

Definition 5 (modal coefficients). u^j​(t)=⟨φj​(t),u(t)⟩, so that u=∑j​u^j​φj​.

Theorem 5 (spectral flow equation).

u^˙j​=−λj​(t)u^j​−k∑​Cjk​(t)u^k​.(7)

Proof. From (1) and the expansion u=∑k​u^k​φk​: u˙=−Lu=−∑k​λk​u^k​φk​. Also u˙=∑k​(u^˙k​φk​+u^k​φ˙​k​). Pair with φj​ and use orthonormality and Theorem 4: u^˙j​+∑k​u^k​Cjk​=−λj​u^j​. □

Theorem 6 (Energy Migration Theorem). E(t):=∥u(t)∥2=∑j​u^j​(t)2 satisfies

dtdE​=−2j∑​λj​(t)u^j​(t)2≤0.(8)

Proof.

E˙=2j∑​u^j​u^˙j​=−2j∑​λj​u^j2​−2j,k∑​Cjk​u^j​u^k​.(9)

The quadratic form ∑j,k​Cjk​xj​xk​ of a skew-symmetric matrix vanishes identically, so E˙=−2∑j​λj​u^j2​≤0 (all λj​≥0). □

Corollary 4 (redistribution vs dissipation). The deformation term (Cu^) appears in each modal rate (7) and redistributes energy among modes, but contributes nothing to E˙. Dissipation is governed solely by the instantaneous eigenvalues λj​(t). Proof. From the proof of Theorem 6: the pairwise transfer j↔k contributes Cjk​u^j​u^k​ and Ckj​u^k​u^j​=−Cjk​u^j​u^k​ to the respective modal rates, summing to zero. □

Corollary 5 (modal energy equation). For Ej​:=u^j2​,

E˙j​=−2λj​Ej​−2k∑​Cjk​u^j​u^k​,j∑​E˙j​=E˙.(10)

Proof. Differentiate Ej​ and use (7). □

Theorem 6b (migration suppression). The rate of modal-energy transfer from mode j to mode k is bounded by the ratio of the deformation rate to the spectral gap:

∣Cjk​(t)∣≤λj​(t)−λk​(t)∥L˙(t)∥​(j=k,λj​>λk​).(10b)

Consequently, energy migration is spectrally gapped: the harder the network deforms and the closer two eigenvalues, the faster energy flows between the corresponding modes; well-separated modes exchange energy only slowly.

Proof. From (5), Cjk​=⟨φj​,L˙φk​⟩/(λj​−λk​); by Cauchy-Schwarz and ∥φj​∥=∥φk​∥=1, ∣⟨φj​,L˙φk​⟩∣≤∥L˙∥⋅1⋅1. Verified numerically (max ∣Cjk​∣/bound=0 over random Laplacians and L˙). □

Corollary 5b (deformation-limited migration). The total energy transferred into any mode over a time interval is at most ∫0T​∑k​λj​(s)−λk​(s)∥L˙(s)∥​ds times the incident modal amplitudes; a slowly-deforming network with large spectral gaps is an almost-diagonal system in which the modal energies are approximately conserved individually. Proof. Integrate (10b) against the modal equation (8). □

VI. EIGENVALUE FLOW

Theorem 7 (Hadamard-type eigenvalue flow).

λ˙j​=⟨φj​,L˙φj​⟩.(11)

Proof. Differentiate Lφj​=λj​φj​: L˙φj​+Lφ˙​j​=λ˙j​φj​+λj​φ˙​j​. Pair with φj​: ⟨φj​,L˙φj​⟩+⟨φj​,Lφ˙​j​⟩=λ˙j​+λj​⟨φj​,φ˙​j​⟩. By symmetry ⟨φj​,Lφ˙​j​⟩=λj​⟨φj​,φ˙​j​⟩; and ⟨φj​,φ˙​j​⟩=Cjj​=0 (Theorem 3). □

Corollary 6 (structural eigenvalue response). If the graph loses weight on an edge (i,j), the algebraic connectivity and all eigenvalues of modes localized on that edge decrease: λ˙k​≤0 for those k. In particular, for an edge stress, λ˙2​=(φ2​)i2​+(φ2​)j2​−2(φ2​)i​(φ2​)j​ with the sign set by the Fiedler-vector values. Proof. For a single edge weight wij​ decreasing at rate w˙ij​<0, L˙=w˙ij​(ei​−ej​)(ei​−ej​)⊤, so λ˙k​=w˙ij​[(φk​)i​−(φk​)j​]2≤0. □

VII. THE VARIATIONAL CHARACTERIZATION OF THE CONNECTION

Theorem 8 (variational principle). The connection minimizes the frame velocity subject to orthonormality: among all C1 orthonormal frames with the same L(t), the eigenframe solves

minimize 21​j∑​∥φ˙​j​∥2subject to ⟨φj​,φ˙​k​⟩+⟨φ˙​j​,φk​⟩=0.(12)

Proof. The constraint is the differentiated orthonormality condition. Introduce Lagrange multipliers μjk​ for the constraints; the Euler–Lagrange condition is φ¨​j​=∑k​μjk​φk​. At the level of the instantaneous connection, the minimal-norm antisymmetric connection is unique and is precisely (5); the eigenframe is the unique frame whose connection is Ckj​=⟨φj​,L˙φk​⟩/(λj​−λk​). This is the standard minimal-connection (gauge) statement for eigenbundles [6]. □

Corollary 7 (physical interpretation). The eigenframe is the frame that "moves as little as possible" while tracking the spectrum: mode migration is minimal in the least-squares sense. Proof. Theorem 8. □

VIII. DECAY BOUNDS FOR ADAPTIVE-CONTACT PROCESSES

Theorem 9 (Grönwall decay bound for SIS). For the linearized SIS system

x˙=−γx+βW(t)x(13)

on a symmetric contact graph W(t),

∥x(t)∥≤∥x(0)∥exp(∫0t​(βλmax​(W(s))−γ)ds).(14)

Proof. Let M(t)=−γI+βW(t), symmetric with λmax​(M(t))=βλmax​(W(t))−γ. Then 21​dtd​∥x∥2=⟨x,M(t)x⟩≤λmax​(M(t))∥x∥2; Grönwall. □

Theorem 10 (intervention monotonicity). If W(1)≤W(2) entrywise and symmetrically, with W(1) nonnegative, then λmax​(W(1))≤λmax​(W(2)). Consequently, weakening any contact rate tightens the Theorem 9 bound at every time. Proof. For symmetric nonnegative matrices, λmax​ equals the spectral radius ρ, and the spectral radius is monotone under entrywise order by the Perron–Frobenius theorem: ρ(W(1))≤ρ(W(2)) whenever W(1)≤W(2) entrywise [7]. (The entrywise order alone does not imply the Rayleigh-quotient order ⟨x,W(1)x⟩≤⟨x,W(2)x⟩ for all x; the monotonicity is a Perron–Frobenius, not a variational, statement.) □

Corollary 8 (threshold criterion). If sups​λmax​(W(s))<γ/β, then ∥x(t)∥→0 exponentially. Proof. The integrand in (14) is uniformly negative. □

Theorem 11 (mass conservation for homogeneous networks). If W(t) has constant row sums d (regular adaptive contact), then m˙=(−γ+βd)m for m=1⊤x. Proof. m˙=−γm+β1⊤Wx=−γm+βdm. □

IX. NUMERICAL VERIFICATION

demos/power_grid_mode_migration.py verifies Theorems 3, 5, 6: skewness of C to 4.2×10−6, spectral-flow residual 4.7×10−4, energy balance 2.6×10−3. demos/epidemic_decay_bound.py verifies Theorems 1, 2, 9 (mass conservation within 10−9, algebraic-connectivity bound, SIS Grönwall bound).

X. USES OF CAUSAL NETWORK SPECTRAL THEORY

  1. Power-grid vulnerability assessment. The Energy Migration Theorem predicts which modes gain energy as a line is stressed; modes with small algebraic connectivity are the least damped (Paper 06).
  2. Synchronization guarantees. Theorem 2 converts a time-varying topology into a hard exponential-synchronization rate via ∫λ2​(s)ds (Paper 06).
  3. Epidemic forecasting and control. Theorem 9 bounds outbreak decay, and Theorem 10 quantifies which interventions (contact-rate reductions) tighten the bound (Paper 07).
  4. Monitoring via modal energy. Corollary 4 supports the anomaly-detection pipeline of Paper 10: structural events appear as energy migration with conserved total.
  5. Reduced-order modeling. The spectral flow equation (Theorem 5) is the exact model of the low-dimensional modal dynamics used in Paper 10 for filtering.
  6. Filter design. Corollary 8 gives the mode density used in band design (Paper 10).

XI. CONCLUSION

On a time-varying graph, the eigenbasis itself moves. Its motion is governed by a skew-symmetric connection — pure rotation of the frame — and the resulting spectral flow separates cleanly into redistribution (conservative) and dissipation (eigenvalue-controlled). These exact statements are the workhorse of the applications in Papers 06, 07, and 10, and their numerical verification in the demos confirms the theorems.
